s: You're listening to Short Wave from NPR.
I want to know, have you heard of this winter arc trend?
我想知道，你听说过这个冬季弧形趋势吗？
SPEAKER 1: Here are some of my winter arc rules that you need to follow.
您需要遵守我的冬季规则。
SPEAKER 2: Welcome back to the winter arc.
SPEAKER 3: What is a winter arc?
And why should I even do one?
So I confess, I had not until recently.
所以我承认，直到最近，我没有。
But I got an education looking on social media, and I got to say, I'm into it.
但我在社交媒体上得到了教育，我必须说，我喜欢它。
Yeah, so the winter arc, it's a self-improvement challenge where people try to get into their best shape and be their best self in the three months leading up to the New Year.
是的，所以冬季的弧线，在新年前三个月里，人们试图保持最佳状态，成为自己。
And often, this is through exercise.
So I guess, I'm already behind.
所以我想，我已经落后了。
Haven't touched a barbell in a minute.
我一分钟都没有碰到一个。
But hearing about this challenge, it got me curious about exercise in the winter.
但听到这个挑战，让我对冬季运动感到好奇。
Like, should we be ramping up our movement in a time when our bodies may naturally be slowing down?
在我们身体自然放缓的时候，我们应该加快运动吗？
And I know you have done some reporting on this, the intersection of exercise and circadian rhythms.
我知道你已经做了一些关于运动和昼夜节律的交叉报告。
I've been reporting on research that's devoted to understanding how exercise is intertwined with our rhythms, including these little clocks that are in our muscles--
我一直在报道关于研究，致力于了解运动是如何与我们的节奏交织在一起的，包括这些小钟在我们的肌肉中--
--though the researchers I talked to hadn't actually heard of the term "winter arc" before.
虽然我和他们谈过的研究人员以前从来没有听说过"冬季弧"这个词。
OK, well, today on the show, is today the day you start your winter arc?
好吧，今天在节目上，今天是你开始冬季的节目吗？
We get into the science behind this exercise trend, the clocks in your muscles, and what you can do to make your winter exercise routine work for you.
我们了解了这种运动趋势背后的科学，肌肉中的钟表，以及你能做些什么来让你的冬季运动习惯适合你。
You're listening to Short Wave, the science podcast from NPR.
你正在听NPR的科学播客"短波".
OK, Will, I want to go back to something you said before the break.
好吧，威尔，我想回到你在休息前所说的话。
You said that muscles have their own clocks, like little watches?
你说肌肉有自己的钟表，像小钟表？
I mean, our brain has the big watch, the central timekeeper.
我的意思是，我们的大脑有一个大手表，
And this is called the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
Yeah, and whether we're talking about the muscles or cells in our liver, our pancreas, our guts, nearly all the cells in our body, they all have their own timekeepers.
无论是肝脏的肌肉还是细胞，胰腺，肠道，我们身体的几乎所有细胞都有自己的计时器。
And those make up our circadian rhythms.
它们构成我们的昼夜节奏。
OK, so nearly all the cells in our body have their own clocks independent from our brain.
好吧，我们身体中的几乎所有细胞都拥有独立于大脑的钟表。
And that's what gives our bodies multiple circadian rhythms.
这就是为我们的身体提供多个昼夜节律的原因。
And circadian rhythms are just the fluctuations in our body that are following loosely a 24-hour clock.
周日节奏只是我们身体的波动，
And these rhythms are controlled by our genes, turning things on and off, and regulating all kinds of key functions in the cells.
这些节奏由我们的基因控制，启动和关闭，调节细胞中的各种关键功能。
So take the clocks in our pancreas.
They're involved in the production of insulin, which changes over the course of the day.
他们参与了胰岛素的生产，在一天的时间里，它变化。
The ones in the liver are helping regulate blood glucose or how you metabolize certain drugs.
肝脏中的药物有助于调节血糖，
The clocks are really guiding these rhythms on a cellular level, which is pretty cool.
在细胞层面上，钟表确实指导这些节奏，这相当酷。
Let's talk about the clocks in our muscles.
让我们谈谈我们的肌肉中的钟表。
How are they doing what they do?
他们如何做他们的工作？
Yeah, there's this very intricate circadian dance that happens throughout the 24-hour cycle in our muscles.
是的，有一种非常复杂的昼夜舞蹈在我们的肌肉中发生在24小时周期内。
And one way to think about it is, just like we have periods of time when, you know, we need to rest and then when we're more active, the same goes for our muscle cells.
一种思考方式是，就像我们有时，你知道的，我们需要休息，然后当我们更活跃的时候，我们的肌肉细胞也是如此。
And these clocks are helping direct all of that.
这些钟表有助于指导所有这些。
For the active phase, I want my muscles to be ready.
为了活跃阶段，我希望我的肌肉准备好。
I want it to have all of its energy stores, like glycogen, things like that, to be all primed.
我希望它拥有所有的能量储备，这样的东西，一切都准备好了。
I want the oxidative metabolism to be ready to go.
我希望氧化代谢准备好。
Yeah, I might be ready to do protein synthesis, but maybe I'll save repair and maintenance to when I'm resting.
是的，我可能准备好做蛋白质合成，但也许我会把维修和维护保存到我休息的时候。
Karyn Esser is the chair of physiology and aging at the University of Florida's College of Medicine.
卡林·埃塞尔是佛罗里达大学医学院生理学和老龄化主任。
And she's done a lot of the pioneering work in this area.
她在这个领域做了很多开创性的工作。
And she says, for example, our muscles are very dense.
她说，例如，我们的肌肉非常密集。
It takes a lot of effort to move proteins around the cell to repair them.
移动蛋白质到细胞周围需要大量的努力来修复它们。
So it just makes sense that you wouldn't try to do that when you're also being very active in using them.
因此，你不应该试图这样做，当你也非常积极地使用它们。
I like the idea that our muscles have their own cycles, because I run marathons, Will.
我喜欢我们的肌肉有自己的循环，因为我跑马拉松，威尔。
And because of these clocks, my muscles know when to use their resources, and they're not trying to repair while I'm in the middle of trying to run a race, sounds like.
由于这些钟表，我的肌肉知道何时使用他们的资源，他们没有试图修复，而我正在试图跑一场比赛。
Going back to the clocks thing, you know how regular clocks and watches can get out of sync--
返回时钟，你知道普通的时钟和时钟如何失调--
Can that happen with our body clocks?
我们的身体时钟能否做到这一点？
I mean, ideally, our clocks are in the same phase, or, as Karyn likes to say, they're in the same time zone.
我的意思是，理想情况下，我们的时钟在同一阶段，或者，像卡林喜欢说的，它们在同一时区。
But that doesn't always happen, right?
但这并不总是发生的，对吧？
Our clocks can get scrambled because of our behavior or our environment.
我们的时钟可能会因为我们的行为或环境而变得乱。
And when that happens, they can become misaligned with clocks elsewhere in the body.
当这种情况发生时，它们可能会与身体其他地方的时钟不一致。
You know, the brain clock thinks it's here, and the liver and the pancreas think it's something else.
你知道的，脑钟认为它在这里，而肝脏和胰腺认为它是别的东西。
And I mean, that's jet lag.
And it just doesn't feel good.
And like I said, I mean, the master timekeeper in the brain responds very strongly to light.
正如我说的，大脑中的时间表表对光非常强烈反应。
I think most people kind of know that.
我认为大多数人都知道这一点。
So when we're traveling to a new place and getting light at a different time, it takes your body time to adjust.
所以当我们去一个新的地方，在不同的时间得到光时，你的身体需要时间来适应。
But our other organs can also struggle, right?
但我们的其他器官也可以扎，对吧？
Your body is just kind out of whack.
--this isn't just when we travel to a new time zone, you know, with jet lag.
这不仅仅是当我们旅行到一个新的时区，你知道的，随着飞行延迟。
I mean, there's social jet lag, which is just when you deviate from your normal schedule on the weekends.
我的意思是，有社交拖延，当你周末偏离正常的时间表时。
Maybe you stay up too late and sleep in.
We can misalign our clocks through all kinds of behaviors in our daily life, you know, when we--
我们可以通过日常生活中的各种行为，你知道，当我们--
I don't know what you're talking about, Will.
我不知道你在说什么，威尔。
你不是一个深夜的零食者吗？
I love string cheese at midnight.
And then, you know, blasting the bright light on you at the same time, right?
然后，你知道的，同时向你发射了光明的光线，对吧？
--surefire way to mess up your clocks.
I mean, there's actually a lot of research showing when your body clocks are not in sync, it's bad for your health.
很多研究表明，当你的身体时钟不同步时，这对你的健康有害。
Circadian misalignment is associated with health conditions like diabetes, cardiovascular disease, psychiatric illness, and more.
循环不适应性与糖尿病，心血管疾病，精神疾病等健康状况有关。
And this is actually why night-shift workers are more at risk of these diseases.
这就是为什么夜班工作者更容易患上这些疾病的原因。
And experiments in healthy people have even shown that if you mess up their clocks enough, you can pretty quickly wreak havoc on, you know, their metabolism, blood sugar, and so on.
在健康人身上进行的实验甚至表明，如果你足够乱他们的钟表，你可以很快破坏他们的代谢，血糖等。
Wow, I am convinced I need to clean up my sleep.
我相信我需要清理自己的睡眠。
So these clocks being as aligned as possible is, clearly, very important.
因此，这些钟表尽可能一致，显然是非常重要的。
Let's talk about how that connects to exercise and the winter arc.
让我们谈谈如何与运动和冬季弧度联系起来。
Because in the winter, you are getting less of that light cue to regulate the clock in your brain.
因为在冬季，你会得到更少的光线信号来调节你的大脑的时钟。
Should you be getting less exercise in the winter months?
你应该在冬季减少运动吗？
Like, what should be the approach to exercise in the winter?
冬季运动应该是什么样的？
OK, so definitely stay active during winter months and keep exercising, even when there's less light out, because some exercise is better than none, right?
好吧，所以一定要在冬季保持活跃，继续炼，即使在外面有较少的光线，因为一些炼比没有炼好，对吧？
You're not going to let people off the hook--
You can actually make an argument that exercise is especially important this time of year because it can serve as a very strong cue for your circadian rhythms.
你实际上可以说运动是特别重要的，因为它可以作为一个非常强烈的指标，
Yeah, because light is not the only input for the circadian system.
是的，因为光不是 circadian系统的唯一输入。
And so is exercise, which means, when we're active and exercising, that can actually help shift the timing of your body clocks.
运动也是如此，这意味着，当我们活跃和炼时，这实际上可以帮助改变身体钟表的时间。

In lab experiments, when human muscle cells not attached to a brain are shocked to kind of mimic twitches and, you know, what happens during exercise, that's enough to change the settings of the muscle clocks.
在实验室实验中，当没有连接到大脑的人类肌肉细胞被震惊时，你知道，运动期间发生的事情，这足以改变肌肉钟的设置。
Yeah, and animal studies from Karyn and others suggest exercise can even override the influence of the brain clock and, you know, activate your muscles at a particular time.
是的，卡林和其他人的动物研究表明运动甚至可以取消大脑时钟的影响，你知道，在特定的时间激活你的肌肉。
What do you mean by that?
So the brain clock sticks closely to the light.
因此，大脑时钟紧贴着光。
You know, that's what it follows.
你知道，这就是其后的结果。
But the muscle clocks, not as much.
And the evidence actually supports the idea that you can train these clocks in your muscles.
而证据实际上支持这样一个观点，即你可以在肌肉中训练这些钟表。
They are responsive to when you exercise, and they will catch on over time.
他们会随着时间的推移感受你的运动。

And that's why consistency is probably one of the biggest practical takeaways for people from all this work, meaning you want to do your best to stick to a pretty regular of exercise day to day because your muscles will be ready at that time of day.
这就是为什么连贯性可能是人们从这项工作中获得的最大实用训练之一，这意味着你想尽最大努力坚持日常运动，因为你的肌肉在那个时候就准备好了。
Now, the clocks are not, like, totally precise, so don't stress about doing it at the exact minute every day.
现在，钟表不是完全精确的，所以不要压力每天的确切时刻。
The idea is to shoot for, Karyn says, roughly, about the same two to three-hour window because that's when your muscles will be ready to go.
卡林说，目标是拍摄，大约是两到三个小时的时间，因为那时你的肌肉就准备好了。
That is a good tip, exercising at the same time, though, is there a perfect time, like a best time, to work out?
这是一个好提示，同时运动，然而，有没有一个完美的时间，像一个最好的时间，做运动吗？。
Yeah, I mean, it's a big question.
是的，这是一个很大的问题。
I mean, put simply, science has not settled on kind of one ideal time to exercise.
简单地说，科学还没有确定运动的理想时间。
The studies in this area tend to have lots of caveats, like which groups are you looking at, who's being studied.
在这个领域的研究往往有很多警告，比如你正在研究哪些群体，谁正在研究。
The kind of exercise they're doing can vary.
他们所做的运动可能有所不同。
And all of this makes it hard to give kind of universal advice.
所有这些都使得很难提供普遍的建议。
And along with that, I mean, there's a question of, like, what are your goals with exercise?
另外，我们还要问，你的运动目标是什么？
If you care about peak performance, like when you're going to do your best, the human data does point toward the afternoon.
如果你关心最高绩效，比如你要尽最大努力的时候，人类数据确实指向下午。
And I spoke to Raphael Knaier about this.
我和拉斐尔·克奈尔谈到了这个问题。
He's an exercise physiologist at the University of Basel in Switzerland.
他是瑞士巴塞尔大学的运动生理学家。
So he reviewed the evidence a few years ago and said, yes, afternoon did come out on top.
几年前，他检查了证据，并说，是的，下午确实出现了。
I like exercising in the afternoon.
Why did it come out on top--
I mean, scientists have speculated that everything from shifts in core body temperature to hormones, to neural activation, all of this could be responsible for this morning to afternoon variation.
科学家们猜测，从核心体温变化到激素，到神经激活，所有这些都可能导致今天早上到下午的变化。
Your muscle clocks could be involved.
你的肌肉时钟可能会受到影响。
But Raphael says it's really not settled yet.
但拉斐尔说，它还没有解决。
Just because the afternoon is the best time on average over a certain population, does not mean that it's the best time for every individual, that we found large inter-individual differences.
只是因为下午是一个特定人口的平均最佳时间，这并不意味着这是每个人的最佳时间，我们发现了很大的个人间差异。
Yeah, so the quality of these studies vary.
所以这些研究的质量有所不同。

And this is why scientists are kind of reticent to make declarations around the best time to exercise, although it does seem like the afternoon is when kind of elite athletes tend to break the most world records.
这就是为什么科学家们不愿意做出关于运动最好的时间的声明，虽然似乎是下午时，精英运动员倾向于打破世界纪录。
Well, so if I have the best chance of getting my best mile, I should do it in the afternoon.
所以，如果我有最好的机会，我应该在下午做。
Assuming you've been training in the afternoon as well, yeah.
假设你也在下午训练，是的。
So to that point, the best advice for exercising in the winter months, what is it?
所以到那个时候，冬季运动的最佳建议是什么？。
Yeah, so, I mean, first, like we mentioned, you know, be consistent whenever you work out.
是的，所以，我的意思是，首先，正如我们所提到的，你知道的，每当你炼时都保持一致。
I mean, studies have found that exercising in the morning or early afternoon can push your circadian rhythms toward an earlier schedule.
研究表明，在早上或早下午炼可以推动您的昼夜节奏转向更早的时间表。
--for this is advancing your body clocks.
因为这就是提升你的身体时钟。
So you'll want to go to bed earlier naturally and wake up earlier if you--
所以你自然会想早点睡觉，早点醒来，如果你...
I mean, this is what Shawn Youngstedt found in his study.
这就是肖恩·扬斯泰特在他的工作室发现的。
He's an exercise scientist at Arizona State University.
他是亚利桑那州立大学的运动科学家。
Well, let's say, you know, someone has an issue where they're having a delayed body clock, being a night owl.
让我们说，你知道的，有人有一个问题，他们有一个延迟的身体时钟，
People are staying up more later now.
We can say, OK, well, you might want to get exercise in the morning, but it also might benefit you if you get it in, in the afternoon, perhaps help you advance your body clock.
我们可以说，好吧，你可能会想在早上做运动，但如果你得到它，也可能会有益于你，在下午，也许可以帮助你提升你的身体时钟。
So that's something to keep in mind at this time of year, you know, if you're really trying to stay on a good schedule.
所以，你应该记住这个时候，如果你真的想保持良好的时间表。
And even if the sun is not up yet, you can exercise in the morning and be active, and that will certainly influence your clocks.
即使太阳还没有升起，你早上可以炼，这肯定会影响你的钟表。
Or, if you're not a morning person, you can prioritize the early afternoon.
或者，如果你不是早晨的人，你可以优先考虑早下午。
You know, it does get more complicated because some people have different chronotypes, meaning, you know, some people have a kind of genetic predisposition toward being a night owl or an early riser.
你知道，它变得更加复杂，因为一些人有不同的时间型，这意味着，你知道，一些人有一种遗传倾向于成为夜猫或早起。
Those things can also kind of influence our circadian rhythms.
这些东西也会影响我们的昼夜节奏。
But all of us should be exercising--
Don't wait till the New Year.
Will Stone, thank you so much for being our exercise coach in this episode of Short Wave.
威尔·斯通，谢谢你成为我们的练习教练。

Before we go, if you've ever been curious to see what we all get up to at NPR headquarters in person, I have good news for you because you're the public in public media, and you can enter for a chance to go behind the scenes at NPR headquarters.
在我们离开之前，如果你有兴趣看到我们在NPR总部亲自做什么，我对你有好消息，因为你是公众媒体的公众，在NPR总部，你可以走进幕后。
One lucky winner will come tour the building in Washington, DC, watch a live taping of All Things Considered, and have lunch with an NPR journalist.
一位幸运的赢家会来参观华盛顿的建筑，查看"一切考虑"的现场录像，和一个NPR记者一起吃午饭。
It's going to be so fun.
And it's free to enter at npr.org/giveaway.
在 npr.org/giveaway上可以免费访问。
And when you're on that website, you can make a donation for more entries and support the NPR network while you're at it.
当你进入这个网站时，您可以捐赠更多作品，并在此期间支持NPR网络。
Of course, there's no purchase or donation required to enter.
当然，不需要购买或捐赠才能进入。
You just have to be 18 years or older.
You can find links to the entry page and official rules at npr.org/giveaway.
您可以在npr.org/giveaway找到入口页面和官方规则的链接。
And you have until Tuesday, December 1.
你有时间到12月1日星期二。

这集是由伯利·麦科伊制作的。

它是由Rebecca Ramirez编辑的，并由Tyler Jones检查。
